desc:
A cleaner enters the matrix through any cell of the top row and processes the rows one after another. In every row it arrives at some column a (in the top row it may choose a freely), then walks horizontally along that row to some column b (possibly b = a), visiting every cell between a and b inclusive, and pays the value of each of these cells exactly once. Then it steps down into the cell (next row, b). In the last row it stops after its horizontal walk.

Return the smallest total that can be paid. Values may be negative.
hints: Treat one row at a time. What does the next row need to know about everything that happened above it?

Only the column where the cleaner leaves the row. Let f[r][b] be the cheapest total after finishing the walk in row r and standing in column b. Then f[r][b] = min over a of f[r-1][a] + (sum of row r from column a to column b), with f[-1][a] = 0.

Use prefix sums P of the row. For a ≤ b the cost is f[r-1][a] - P[a] + P[b+1], so keep a running minimum of f[r-1][a] - P[a] from the left. For a ≥ b it is f[r-1][a] + P[a+1] - P[b], handled by a running minimum from the right. Take the smaller of the two for each b.
editorial: The row is the stage and the exit column is the state, so f[r][b] is the cheapest way to finish row r in column b. The transition enumerates the entry column a: you pay the contiguous segment between a and b, and the previous row must have ended in column a (the step down keeps the column). Done naively this is O(n2) per row.

With prefix sums P[x] = row[0] + ... + row[x-1], the segment sum is P[b+1] - P[a] when a ≤ b and P[a+1] - P[b] when a ≥ b. Each is a sum of a term depending only on a and a term depending only on b, so the minimum over a is a prefix minimum (from the left) or a suffix minimum (from the right). That reduces each row to O(n). The answer is the minimum of the last row's f. Total O(m · n) time and O(n) space.
